title: Strategic Stability and the Rebuilding of Xi’s Military
gist: Xi's purges have hollowed out the PLA high command (only 6 of 27 full-general posts filled, most of the 2022 Central Military Commission removed), so Beijing needs the U.S.-China 'strategic stability' truce as multi-year cover to rebuild. The authors argue the truce is worth more to Beijing than to Washington, which should extract concessions now (pricing export-control relief beyond Nvidia's H200, releasing the delayed $14 billion Taiwan arms package, testing Taiwan contact limits) before a rebuilt PLA and a hardened 'stability' norm trap the next administration.

insights.claim: Of the seven-member Central Military Commission Xi Jinping selected in 2022, only Zhang Shengmin remains alongside him; Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were formally removed on Aug. 28, 2026, He Weidong and Miao Hua were expelled, and two former defense ministers got suspended death sentences in May.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Near-term PLA war-readiness is degraded, which lowers the probability of a Taiwan conflict over the next 1-3 years.

insights.claim: Only six of the 27 full general or admiral posts in the PLA and People's Armed Police have a confirmed occupant, with lieutenant generals running about 20 in an acting capacity, which leaves an officer corps gripped by psychological paralysis.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: An unproven command chain means China is unlikely to risk a major crisis; supports a lower near-term Taiwan risk premium.

insights.claim: Rocket Force graft left some missiles filled with water and many silo lids inoperable, and on Aug. 24, 2026 the PLA procurement service opened a public tip line for Rocket Force procurement irregularities, which suggests internal channels no longer suffice.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: China's strategic missile force credibility is impaired for now; expect years of re-procurement and refit spending.

insights.claim: Stalin's 1937-38 Great Purge, which repressed over half of 1,844 general-grade officers, led to heavy Soviet losses in the Winter War but the Red Army rebuilt within a few years, so a purged PLA can also rebuild quickly and emerge stronger.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: The PLA weakness window is temporary; do not extrapolate current Taiwan calm beyond about 3 years.

themes.theme: Truce as cover for the rebuild

insights.claim: Most observers read the U.S.-China truce economically, but its overlooked military function is to give a leadership-depleted PLA cover to repair itself, so Xi needs the truce more urgently than economic data suggest.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Beijing's bargaining position is weaker than it looks, which may mean more Chinese concessions on trade and tech in the near term.
insights.quote: The sweeping purge makes Xi need this truce far more urgently than the economic data alone would suggest.

insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: The U.S. rhetorical de-escalation is a regime shift in China risk sentiment; watch for reversal signals.

insights.claim: The PLA broke its three-year pattern of large first-half exercises around Taiwan (April 2023, May 2024, April 2025) with none in 2026, and by August 2026 monthly ADIZ incursions were below half of August 2024 and 2025 levels, a lull that began when Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were put under investigation in January.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Lower visible military activity reflects operational necessity, not goodwill; don't read it as durable de-risking of Taiwan.

insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Undersea cable and shipping disruption risks persist even in a calm period; relevant to telecom infrastructure and insurers.

insights.claim: China's military budget rose about 7 percent this year, the slowest since 2021, and slower budgets plus vacant senior posts mean the PLA will likely miss its 2027 centenary goals.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: The '2027 Taiwan window' narrative is overstated; the risk horizon shifts later.

insights.claim: The authors agree with Amanda Hsiao and Bonnie Glaser that China is not seeking war near term, but argue that once the PLA is rebuilt, and with gray-zone returns diminishing and the 2049 rejuvenation deadline tied to Taiwan, Xi will ultimately use the military.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Long-dated Taiwan conflict risk stays elevated; favors structural defense and supply-chain diversification away from Taiwan.

insights.claim: A Ministry of State Security-linked think tank, CICIR, described U.S.-China competition in May as 'a new phase of strategic stalemate', protracted-war language in which the weaker side uses the pause to build strength, which implicitly concedes that China is the weaker side today.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
entities: China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations
insights.so_what: Beijing sees the truce as a tactical pause, not a settlement, so expect competition to re-intensify later.
insights.quote: a new phase of strategic stalemate
insights.locator: The China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations

themes.theme: Stability framework traps the next administration

insights.claim: Beijing says 'strategic stability' will guide relations for three years and beyond, a horizon that reaches into the next U.S. president's first year and appears in Xi's summit readout but not the White House fact sheet.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Implies a 2026-2029 calm window by Beijing's own framing; the end of the PLA rebuild is a risk inflection.

insights.claim: The framework binds Washington through accumulation (each unimposed tariff or export control becomes a record), frequency (repeating a hollow slogan until it looks like a standing arrangement) and pre-assigned blame (any future tariff, export control or Taiwan arms sale is cast as 'breaking the stability').
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Future U.S. tightening on China tech or tariffs will be framed as escalation, which raises the political cost of reversals and favors a sticky status quo.
insights.locator: The first is accumulation, salami slicing

insights.claim: Concessions are asymmetrically hard to reverse: export licenses become precedents, deferred arms production slots cannot be reclaimed, and chips shipped while export rules were loose stay in China even if the rules are later tightened.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Loosened AI-chip exports during the truce are a permanent capability transfer; relevant to the long-term China AI competitiveness thesis.
insights.quote: Washington can tighten the rule again in a week, and whatever shipped while the rule was loose stays in China.
insights.locator: A new administration can disown the slogan

insights.claim: Washington cleared Nvidia's H200 for China in January 2026 with a 25 percent cut for the U.S. government, and the authors argue any license beyond the H200 should be priced for concrete Chinese concessions.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Further Nvidia China licenses beyond the H200 are likely to be transactional and conditional; China AI-chip revenue remains a policy-gated upside.
insights.locator: First, raise the price of export-control relief

insights.claim: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testified in May that a $14 billion Taiwan arms package was delayed to conserve munitions for the war with Iran, which is draining finite stockpiles and pulling assets from the Indo-Pacific.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Munitions scarcity from the Iran war is constraining Taiwan deliveries, a tailwind for munitions producers and capacity expansion.
insights.locator: Second, clear the paused arms package

insights.claim: Because Beijing cannot afford a major cross-Strait crisis during the rebuild, Washington should probe unwritten limits on Taiwan contact (cabinet visits to Taipei, transits by Taiwan's leaders, visible U.S. training), starting with low-stakes one-off moves.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Possible U.S.-Taiwan signaling events could create headline volatility even in a truce period.

insights.claim: With Xi due at the White House on Sept. 24 and China's rare-earth export-control suspension expiring Nov. 10, 2026, Beijing is likely to offer rare earths as the price for another stretch of quiet.
insights.speaker: Christopher Nye and Charles Sun
insights.so_what: Nov. 10 is a key date for rare-earth supply risk; a suspension extension is likely to be traded for U.S. restraint.
insights.locator: Xi is due at the White House
